nameStory: The blue runner gets its name from the distinctive blue stripe that runs along its body and its habit of constantly moving in swift schools. These energetic fish seem to never stop 'running' through the water, earning them a reputation as one of the ocean's most active swimmers.
description: The blue runner is a sleek, torpedo-shaped fish in the jack family that's built for speed and endurance. These silvery fish sport a characteristic blue stripe along their sides and typically grow to about 14 inches long, though they can reach up to 28 inches. They're schooling fish that you'll often see moving in tight groups, and they're known for their impressive stamina and aggressive feeding behavior.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Look for the telltale blue stripe running along the upper body from head to tail, contrasting with silvery sides that feel smooth and slightly slippery when handled

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Torpedo-shaped and compressed from side to side, with a streamlined profile that feels firm and muscular to the touch

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Two separate dorsal fins with the rear one much longer, and a deeply forked tail fin that's stiff and powerful when fresh

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Terminal mouth positioned at the front tip of the head with small, sharp teeth that feel like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Most commonly 8-14 inches in New England waters, though larger specimens up to 28 inches are possible

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found around reefs, wrecks, and offshore structures, often in schools that create a shimmering wall of silver in the water

habitat: In New England waters, blue runners are typically found around offshore reefs, shipwrecks, and man-made structures like oil rigs and bridge pilings. Juveniles prefer shallower areas near shore, often around rocky reefs and jetties, while adults venture into deeper offshore waters. They're most common in the warmer months when they follow baitfish into our region's waters.

seasonality.spring: Blue runners begin appearing in New England waters as temperatures warm, often first spotted around offshore structures and deeper reefs.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for blue runners, when they're most abundant and active. Schools are commonly seen around wrecks and reefs, aggressively feeding on baitfish.
seasonality.fall: Still present but beginning to move toward warmer waters. This is often when the largest specimens are caught before their southern migration.
seasonality.winter: Very rare in New England waters, as most have migrated south to warmer regions. Any remaining fish will be in the deepest, warmest water available.

funFact: Blue runners are such efficient swimmers that they can maintain their cruising speed for hours without rest, and they've been observed following ships for days at a time, apparently using the vessel's wake to reduce their swimming effort by up to 30%!
confusionNotes: Blue runners are most easily confused with crevalle jacks, but blue runners have a much more prominent blue stripe and lack the crevalle's distinctive black spot on the gill cover. Remember: 'Blue stripe equals blue runner' - if you see that blue line, you've got your ID.
contextualKnowledge: Blue runners go by many names including 'hardtail jack' and 'bluestripe jack,' which can cause confusion when talking with anglers from different regions. They're also sometimes called 'hardnose' due to their firm, bony head structure.
compareHints: Compared to its close relatives, the blue runner is distinguished by its prominent blue stripe - crevalle jacks lack this blue coloration and have a more golden appearance with a black gill spot, while yellow jacks are, as their name suggests, more yellow overall. Blue runners also tend to be more slender than the stockier crevalle jack.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relatives, the Blue Runner has a more elongated body and lacks the crevalle jack's steep forehead profile, while the Yellow Jack (rare in New England) is more golden overall and has a less compressed body shape.
Compared to the more common crevalle jack, yellow jacks have a more golden coloration and longer jaw that extends past the eye.
